coach_says: White was threatening Qxg6, which is checkmate: the queen checks along g6-f7-e8, d8 is covered by the c6 knight and the e7 knight is protected. Moving the knight from d7 does nothing about that. Before any move, ask what your opponent's last move threatens; here Rf1 brings the rook back so ...Rf7 can block the check and you stay a piece up.
also: bring a piece back to defend

coach_says: Queen against a c-pawn on the seventh is a draw if your king hides in the corner: with your king on a8, ...Qxc7 is stalemate, so Black can never take the pawn. Kc6 walks away from that safe corner, and after ...Qd5+ and ...Qa8 the queen sits in front of the pawn and Black's king comes over to win. Keep the king on a8/b8/b7 next to the pawn and let Black's checks run out.

Black's knight on e5 is pinned to the king on f6 by your queen on d4, and your bishop already attacks it. Instead of cashing in straight away with Bxe5+, which only swaps bishop for knight and lets the rook recapture with check on your king, add another attacker with Nf3. Then the pinned knight falls and your last piece is in play. When a piece is pinned, pile up on it before you take.
concept: pile up on the pinned piece

coach_says: After ...f5 the f-pawn wants to go to f4, and Ng3 puts your knight right where ...f4 kicks it away with gain of time and grabs kingside space for Black. Taking first with exf5 stops that and gives your pieces the e4 square. Before putting a piece on a square, check whether an enemy pawn can attack it next move.

Your knight on c3 was attacked by the rook on f3 and had no defender, and dxc4 left it there, so Rxc3 just wins a piece. You could have swapped it off first with Nxe2+, taking a bishop with check, and then played ...dxc4. When one of your pieces is attacked, deal with it before grabbing a pawn elsewhere.
also: trade the attacked piece with check

coach_says: Both your bishop on c2 and White's knight on d5 were hanging, and in that situation you should usually take first. Qxd5 wins the knight, and after Qxc2 your queen takes g2 and hits the rook on h1, so you come out a pawn up with White's king stuck. Be4 saves the bishop but lets the knight escape to e3, throwing the advantage away.

Qh4+ is a check that goes nowhere: g3 kicks the queen back and you've lost time. Play dxe5 first. If White recaptures fxe5, then Qh4+ g3 Qe4+ forks the king and the h1 rook, so White can't take back easily. Get the move order right so the check comes when it actually wins something.

White's king has no knight on f3 to defend it, and your bishop on d6 already aims at h2. Ng4 brings a second attacker and threatens ...Qh4 with mate on h2, so White has to give up material (after g3 Nxh2 Kxh2 Qh4+ you also pick up the c4 bishop). a5 is a slow move when there was a direct attack. When your bishop hits h2 and the defending knight is gone, look for Ng4 and Qh4.

Your bishop on e3 was attacked by the knight, but you could save it with a gain: Bc5 stops Black castling short and keeps the king stuck in the centre, while the knight on c2 is far from home. If it grabs the rook with ...Nxa1, Bxb7 and Rxf7 follow. Bxb7 instead starts a trade-off that lets Black off the hook. When a piece is attacked, look for a retreat that also does a job.
concept: keep their king in the centre

coach_says: Nxg5 gives a whole knight for two pawns, and there's no follow-up attack to justify it; Black just develops and stays a piece up. Your bishop was attacked by the g5 pawn, so you needed a retreat: the best was c5 first, kicking the d6 bishop so it can't trade on g3, then Bg3. Before sacrificing, ask what you get for the piece beyond the pawns.

Bd7 lets White play Bxc6 and Ne5, putting a strong knight in the centre and leaving you with a passive light-squared bishop behind your own pawns on d5 and c4. Ne7 keeps your knight, avoids the exchange and heads for f5 or g6 where it helps the knight on h5. The difference is positional and hard to see, so treat it as a lesson in which pieces to keep.

Your queen was attacked and had to move, but e6 is a poor square: it blocks your e-pawn and the c8 bishop and stops guarding c7, so Bxc7 wins a pawn, and c4 with d5 can chase the queen again. Qd8 keeps c7 protected and frees your pieces. When you retreat an attacked queen, choose a square that keeps defending and doesn't block your own development.

Your h5 knight was attacked, but instead of retreating you had Nxe4! After Nxe4 exf4 the f4 pawn attacks the e3 bishop and your rook on e8 hits the e4 knight, so you win the piece back with a pawn extra. Nf6 is too slow: White takes on c5 and plays f5 against your king. When you're attacked, look for a capture that creates a bigger threat.

Your g- and h-pawns are your winning chance, and the black pawn on h4 is trying to freeze them. g4! frees them now: if ...hxg3 en passant, h4 gives you a passed h-pawn your rook can push. Kf2 is natural, but it lets Black keep the kingside locked with the bishop eyeing g3. In endgames, think about how you'll make a passed pawn before your pawns get blockaded.

The pawn on e4 was free: no black piece defended it, and Qxe4 takes it while keeping your queen central. Bg3 lets Black play ...Qf5, defending the pawn and offering a queen trade. Before making a quiet move, check whether any enemy pawn or piece is just hanging.

You're a pawn up, and the fastest way to win is to make your rook active: Rd2+ checks and then takes h2 (if the king goes to e3 or f3, ...Rxh2 wins a pawn). Kg6 is a reasonable move but gives White time to coordinate. In rook endings, look for checks that bring your rook to the opponent's second rank where the pawns are.
concept: active rook on the second rank

coach_says: Your bishop was attacked, and Bxe5 was the right way to move it: if fxe5, the d-file is open and Qd4+ forks the king and the rook on c3. Taking with the pawn keeps your bishop on d6 blocking your own queen, so you stay a piece down. When a piece of yours is attacked, check what lines it opens if it moves.
also: clear the line for your queen

coach_says: White's bishop on f3 was attacking b7 with your rook behind it on a8, and nothing defended b7. Bc5 ignores that, so Bxb7 wins a pawn. Castling long solves it at once: the king on c8 protects b7 and your rook lands on the open d-file. Before developing, check what your opponent is threatening.
also: castle long to defend and take the d-file

coach_says: Qg5 doesn't create a real threat that Black has to answer: Black swaps bishops with ...Bxh6 Qxh6, then ...Nf5 hits the queen and it has to go back to d2, so you've lost time while your king is still in the centre and ...c5 is coming. Trading on g7 yourself, or just castling, keeps everything in order. Don't move the queen forward if it can simply be chased back.

Your rook on g3 had to move, but on g5 it relied on the queen on g2 for protection. Ng4+ checks, blocks the g-file so the queen no longer defends g5, and attacks the e5 bishop; if you take with fxg4 then ...Qxg5 wins the rook, so you have to give the exchange. Rg6 was safe and active. When a piece is defended down a line, ask whether an enemy piece can step into that line with check.
